name: Behentrimonium chloride

lead: Behentrimonium chloride is a positively charged fatty-chain compound found in many hair conditioners. It clings to the negatively charged surface of hair and is described as reducing static and tangling.
It is an ingredient, not a stand-alone treatment, and hair-specific clinical trials were not found.

paras: Its charged head group is attracted to hair, while the long 22-carbon tail forms a lubricating layer on the strand.
Described as acceptable in rinse-off products at formulated levels but irritating to skin and eyes in concentrated form, and very toxic to aquatic life.

lead: Behentrimonium chloride (also docosyltrimethylammonium chloride, BTAC-228) is a quaternary ammonium compound that acts as a cationic surfactant. It is a yellow, waxlike solid with the formula C25H54ClN.[1][2]

It is used in cosmetics, chiefly hair conditioners, as an antistatic and conditioning agent; its positively charged head group binds to negatively charged hair surfaces, and its long fatty chain is described as smoothing the hair and reducing static.[1][2]
Published research specific to its hair effects is limited, although studies of conditioner ingredients on hair and a post-marketing safety assessment of leave-on lotions containing it exist.[3][4]

paras: The molecule consists of a 22-carbon chain derived from behenic acid attached to a trimethylammonium group, with a chloride counter-ion; its IUPAC name is N,N,N-trimethyldocosan-1-aminium chloride.[1][2] It has a molar mass of about 404 g/mol.[1][2] The compound is described as poorly soluble in cold water and soluble in hot water.[2]

Wikipedia lists uses as an antistatic agent, a disinfectant in some applications, and an ingredient in conditioners, hair dyes, mousses and detergents.[1] Grokipedia describes its role in conditioners as helping to smooth the cuticle and improve manageability.[2]
Streaming-potential and electrokinetic studies of common conditioner ingredients have examined how cationic agents interact electrostatically with human hair.[3][5]

Grokipedia reports that it is considered acceptable in rinse-off products at concentrations up to 4% when formulated to avoid irritation, may irritate skin and eyes at higher concentrations, and is classed as very toxic to aquatic life.[2] A 2013 paper reported a post-marketing adverse-event analysis of behentrimonium chloride-containing leave-on body lotions in support of their safety.[4] Wikipedia notes laboratory tests indicating ready biodegradability.[1]

No studies found. Related research includes an in vitro and post-marketing safety assessment of leave-on lotions containing the compound,[4] and laboratory electrokinetic studies on hair of conditioner ingredients.[3][5]
